Spring brings raccoon mothers looking for chimneys and soffits to raise young, and summer is bat season in the older housing stock. Most Bridgeport jobs start with a full roofline and foundation inspection, then removal and sealing every entry we find, because closing only the obvious hole rarely holds in these older buildings.

Every job ends with sealing, because Danbury's connected woods and river corridor always have another animal nearby.

Stamford.wildlife_intro:
Stamford gives our crew two very different kinds of jobs. Downtown and the older neighborhoods produce rats, pigeons, and raccoons working dumpsters and older rooflines, while wooded North Stamford produces squirrels, flying squirrels, bats, and woodchucks on large lots that back up to Mianus River Park and other forest. Along the Sound in Shippan and the Cove, skunks and raccoons work the shoreline streets, and gulls and geese gather where lawns meet the water.

North Stamford colonials with complex rooflines are classic squirrel and bat houses: tall trees drop right to the roof, and soffit and gable gaps go unnoticed from the ground. In Springdale and Glenbrook, postwar capes put low rooflines within easy reach of fences and branches. Winter drives rodents into attics across the city, spring brings denning raccoons and skunks under decks, and our crew seals the structure as part of the job so the next animal cannot use the same openings.
